entries.title: Markers for the rest: the map as the game shows it
entries.detail: A third Display toggle beside "Objects as themselves", "Markers for the rest", keeps a marker for every object of a type that has no sprite. Those are the zones, bounds, triggers, spawners and stoppers the game never shows, and the few types the map does not draw yet. It is on by default, so nothing changes until you turn it off; then, with the objects shown as themselves, the map shows only the objects the game shows. A hidden object takes its label, its hover and its wires with it. The object categories keep choosing which objects are on the map at all, so the enemies can still go while the rest stay.

entries.title: Chant orbs, sparks, Zs and hint flies
entries.detail: With the objects shown as themselves, the game's little effects come with them. Sit-chanting Mudokons glow with chant orbs; chiselling Mudokons strike sparks at every stroke, and Exoddus's drills throw them as they bite. Sleeping Slogs, Sligs, crawling Sligs and Fleeches let off rising Zs, and the Zzz spawners breathe them on their own beat. Oddysee's hint flies hover about their spots in twenty little loops. Each is drawn as the game draws it, the orbs and flies as sprites, the sparks and Zs as the engine's own lines, on the game's dice.

entries.title: Labels walk with the creatures
entries.detail: With "Patrols" on, a creature's label and its edited mark go where it goes instead of staying at the spot it was placed; hovering and clicking still work on that spot.

entries.title: A screen's objects start afresh when you arrive
entries.detail: With the objects shown as themselves, every mine, Mudokon and patrol on a path begins from its first frame when the path comes into view. That is how the game starts a screen's objects when it loads, rather than from wherever the clock would have carried them meanwhile. Turning "Objects as themselves" on starts the screen over too, and "Patrols" sends the creatures back to their marks.

entries.title: Slurgs, Greeters, bats, Glukkons and flying Sligs join the patrols
entries.detail: With "Patrols" on, the rest of the creatures that move about do so too. Slurgs creep along their floors and turn back at a bound or an edge. Greeters roll their beat with the laser sweeping ahead of them, stopping now and then for a word. Oddysee's bats hang their while, take off and fly their lines, and flying Sligs patrol their tracks and pause at the ends. Exoddus's Glukkons pace between their bounds with a laugh or a word. Oddysee's background Glukkons speak their lines with the objects shown alone. Every pace, pause and roll is the game's own, from the decomp and the dice table on the disc.

entries.title: Patrols: Sligs, Scrabs, Fleeches and bombs on the move
entries.detail: A second Display toggle, "Patrols" (or press b), lets the creatures that walk their beats walk them, once the objects are shown as themselves. Sligs pace between their bound markers, pause the time their fields give each side, turn on the spot and head back. Scrabs walk or run to their bounds, wait, turn and howl now and then. Awake Fleeches turn about, cry and crawl within their patrol range. The moving bombs that set off at a fresh start follow their tracks and idle at their stoppers. Every stride is the game's own, stepped along the map's collision lines from the brains in the decomp with the game's dice, as an unnoticed Slig would walk it. A creature is drawn wherever it has walked to, while its label stays where it was placed and hovering finds it there. In Oddysee, one whose beat spans two screens steps across the gap between them as Abe does. The toggle sits greyed until the objects are shown and animated.

entries.title: Slogs growl, paramites turn, saws and drills stroke
entries.detail: With the objects shown as themselves, more of the map keeps itself busy the way the game does. Awake Slogs growl and scratch on the timers the game gives them, and patrolling Paramites turn about every few seconds, once in a while drawing back a hiss. Rupture Farms' meat saws stroke down and back and pause between strokes, and Exoddus's drills run their strokes along their rails, each by its own fields. The Fleeches hanging from the ceilings of Necrum and the two vaults sway on their tongues. Every pause and every turn is rolled from the game's own dice table, read off the disc, so no two neighbours keep the same rhythm.

entries.title: Objects as themselves: every sprite as the game draws it
entries.detail: A new Display toggle, "Objects as themselves" (or press o), swaps every object that has a sprite for the sprite it stands in the moment its screen loads. The sprites are read off the discs like the camera art, and placed by the game's own rules: snapped to the grid, dropped onto the floor, scaled, facing its way and tinted for its level. Then it animates at the engine's own pace, for as long as a new setting, "Animate the objects", is left on; off, every sprite stands on its first frame. Mines flash, a UXB blinks the pattern its fields spell, and working Mudokons scrub and chisel, break off and start again as the game's own dice fall, turning around now and then. Sleeping Sligs and Slogs breathe, motion-detector lasers sweep their rooms, portal doves circle and the chime lock's ball bobs. Zones, bounds and the other invisible markers keep their rectangles, hovering and clicking work as before, and an export draws the first frame.

entries.title: The source code moves to RetroAtlas
entries.detail: The map's source code now lives on GitHub under RetroAtlas, beside the other maps in the collection. "About this map" shows the new address, the source link at the foot of every level page leads there too, and the old one forwards to it. It is still this map's own code, and the map itself stays at oddworldmap.com.

entries.title: The ender levels' names read as words
entries.detail: Where a field names an Exoddus level, the six ender levels showed with an underscore stitched into the name, mudanchee vault_ender and brewery_ender among them. They read as words now: mudanchee vault ender, brewery ender and the rest.

entries.title: Four sidebar buttons lose the hover wait
entries.detail: World graph, Export view, Export whole path and By the numbers used the browser's own tooltip: you hovered and waited for it, and on a phone it never appeared at all. They now show the same instant note the Display toggles and Export path as JSON already carry, and a tap reaches it too. The words are the ones they had, tidied to read as sentences.

entries.title: Ten object types read their values in words
entries.detail: A drill's behaviour said 0, 1 or 2; it now says not interactable, toggle or use. A teleporter names the level it sends you to and the wipe it plays. A bell stone says whether it whistles or chimes, an Oddysee hand stone the level each of its three views looks at, and an express well the level it rides to while its switch is off. Slurgs, flying sligs and their spawners gain their start direction, and nine of the ten types the plane they sit on. That is 560 objects across both games, all of them reading raw until now because the decompilation declares these fields one struct deeper than the map's reader looked.

entries.title: Moving bombs and pants lockers say their plane
entries.detail: A moving bomb's plane and its two flags, and the plane on Exoddus' Slig pants lockers, showed as bare 0s and 1s rather than words. The decompilation declares them in two shapes the builder's type reader could not see: one data struct written as a class, and one member spelled with a capital. Oddysee's 35 bombs now read their plane as full and, all but two, their alarm trigger as false; the seven lockers read full as well. The words show with more object fields turned on, in the field picker, in the editor, and in search, which matches on them. The stored values are unchanged, and no marker moved.

entries.title: The three exports fold into one button
entries.detail: Export view, Export whole path and Export path as JSON were three rows at the foot of the Display toggles. One Export button stands there now and opens to the three on a click, a tap or the keyboard, staying open while an export runs so the button you pressed still says what it is doing. The exports themselves are unchanged.

entries.title: Editing waits behind a setting
entries.detail: The Edit objects button no longer sits in the sidebar of every visit. It appears, with its e key, once Settings → Objects and fields → "Edit object properties" is on, beside the other settings for custom-level builders and the curious. Edits you have already made keep applying and keep their marks with the setting off. Its row counts them across both games and forgets them all in two presses, so nothing on the device goes unaccounted for.

entries.title: Undo and redo an edit, one step at a time
entries.detail: Every change you make to an object can be stepped back one at a time, with Ctrl+Z or ⌘Z (Shift for redo, Ctrl+Y or ⌘Y too) or the undo and redo buttons in the edit panel. Putting a whole path back as the disc has it is one step like any other, so a mistaken revert comes back with one press. Each path keeps its own trail for as long as the tab is open; the edits themselves stay on the device as before, and forgetting them all in Settings clears the trail with them.

entries.title: Edits stay on this device between visits
entries.detail: An object you edit is still edited when you come back. The change is kept on this device as its difference from the disc, applied again the moment the map loads, and marked wherever it shows, so a later visit can never mistake it for the game's own data. Settings counts what the device holds and forgets it all in two presses; a path's own revert lives in the edit panel. Should a rebuild of the map move an object out from under an edit, that edit is forgotten and the map says so. An embedded map always shows the disc's data.

entries.title: Edited data says so wherever it shows
entries.detail: Beyond the outline on the marker itself, an edit now announces itself on every surface that reads the object. The tooltip, the screen list and a search hit name the fields you changed, and the path's button and the chip carry a mark. The world graph marks the path's box and says so in its title, and a screen reader hears it with the path. Every export of an edited path says so in its name (the JSON, both images and the graph), so nothing that leaves the page can pass for the game's own data. A copied link still opens on the shipped object, and says so.

entries.title: Edit an object's properties in the browser
entries.detail: Press Edit objects, or e, and click any marker: a panel lists every field the game stores for it. Each is a dropdown of the values the game knows or a number you can type, with what the disc shipped beside anything you changed and a way to put it back. The map follows the edit everywhere at once: a door sent to another camera draws its arrow there, a lever given a new switch id wires up, the tooltip and the screen list read the new value. An edited marker wears a second outline, so nothing you changed can pass for the game's own data.

entries.title: Save a path for the level editor
entries.detail: A third export button hands the path you are looking at over as a file the AliveTeam level editor can open: every object with all of its fields, and every collision line, in the editor's own format. It carries no artwork and no game code, which makes it a description of the path rather than a level, and it is the same file this map is checked against object for object. Open it to read the path, or import it into your own copy of the game to build on it, knowing that the import replaces that path's objects and lines and drops its foreground masks. The button says so before you press it, on hover and to a screen reader alike.

entries.title: Exoddus finally shows its foreground
entries.detail: The foreground masks overlay marks the scenery drawn in front of Abe, and on Exoddus it has been showing almost none of it. The discs store those blocks compressed and pixel-by-pixel, and the map was reading them as something else and giving up a few blocks in. Every Exoddus screen is rebuilt from the discs, which turns 107 thousand marked pixels into 4 million, and seventeen screens that looked as though they had no foreground at all turn out to have plenty. Oddysee was always read correctly and is unchanged.

entries.title: Two Oddysee paths were off by a collision line
entries.detail: The level tables the map reads its offsets from come from the PC release, and two paths on the PlayStation disc disagree with them by a single collision line. To the Stockyards was missing a hoist and a wall, and To the Board Room a continue point, while drawing a stray line along the edge of its first screen. The map now counts the lines off the disc itself and takes the tables' word only where the two agree.

entries.title: The Bonewerkz security claws read their own words
entries.detail: Exoddus' two security claws were showing the wrong numbers: the field before them is four bytes wide rather than two, so everything after it was being read one word early. Both now carry the values the game does.

entries.title: Shadow zones show the colour they cast
entries.detail: A shadow zone tints the sprites on the plane it names, and its three colour fields were being read off the disc and then dropped. Every one of them now carries its red, green and blue, and the plane it tints, alongside the rest, so you can see which zones bite hardest, which barely tint at all, and which reach both planes.

entries.title: The world graph saves as an image
entries.detail: The whole-game diagram now leaves the site as a file: save svg and save png sit beside fit in its own bar. The SVG stays sharp at any size (print it, put it on a wiki) and the PNG pastes anywhere at twice the diagram's actual size. Both carry the diagram with every name on it, plus the title and colour legend across the top, and the filename says which diagram it is: oddworld-ae-graph.svg without the demo copies, oddworld-ae-graph-demos.svg with them.

entries.title: Every level has a plain page of its own
entries.detail: A search for a place by name (Paramonia, the Scrabanian Temple, the SoulStorm Brewery) used to have nowhere to land but the map's front door. Each of the 25 levels now has a plain page under /levels/. It carries what the level is, a representative screen, and its paths in the order you meet them, every one a link that opens the interactive map in the right place. The pages are built from the same data the map draws, so a name or a count can never disagree with it.

entries.title: Wells say which plane they sit on
entries.detail: A well's scale used to read a bare 0 or 1; it now reads full or half, the way a Slig's or a Mudokon's does. Exoddus's Scrab spawner gains the same reading: its spawned Scrab's scale is a plane, and three of its yes/no flags read as words. The games declare these fields on a shared base record the map's builder never looked inside; now it does.

entries.title: A screen lists the objects that belong to it
entries.detail: Both games place objects on a grid slightly larger than the screen you see, and some objects sit in the leftover gap. The screen list and the By-the-numbers screen column used to file those under whichever screen the map happened to draw them over, or under no screen at all. Not one of Oddysee's 111 death-drop zones was filed under its own screen. Every object now counts under the screen it really belongs to, and the counts no longer shift when "Gaps between screens" is flipped. An object drawn over a neighbouring screen still says so: its row keeps the offscreen tag, and its outline stays dotted. Tapping an object opens the screen it belongs to, which need not be the one under your finger.

entries.title: A wrong address gets a proper 404 page
entries.detail: A stale or mistyped link used to land on GitHub's stock error page. It now lands on a small page of the map's own, which says nothing lives there and offers the way back. The map itself was never the problem: every level, path and screen travels after the # in its link, so a missing page only ever means the address in front of it.

entries.title: Timers read in seconds, not just frame counts
entries.detail: Every delay, pause and countdown an object stores is a count of frames, and until now the map showed you the bare number. A Slig's patrol pause said 30. It now says 30 frames ≈ 1s. Its panic timer says 300 frames ≈ 10s, its listening window 90 frames ≈ 3s. The exact count is still there for anyone who cares about the frame, and the reading is there for everyone who just wants to know how long. A hundred and twenty-six timer fields carry it, spread over forty-two kinds of object: sligs, scrabs, paramites, fleeches and slogs, the drills and saws and timed mines, the alarms, the gas countdown, the timers and switch delays. The rate is the engine's own. Exoddus multiplies the mine countdown, the one value the developers themselves labelled in seconds, by thirty, and both games divide their gas-countdown clock by thirty to put a number on screen. Hover a timer's name in a screen list and it says so.

entries.title: A number now says what it measures
entries.detail: Object fields that are plain numbers have always shown as plain numbers, whatever they counted. A few now say what they are measured in. A sleeping Slig's hearing reads 6 grid rather than 6, so it lines up with what the ruler already tells you in grid squares. The chance of a Slig saying "what?" reads 100% rather than 100. A Colourful Meter's mine countdown reads in seconds, the unit the game itself stores it in. One field named for a percentage stays bare, a Slig's chance of beating a Mudokon: it is rolled against 255, so it is not one. "Show raw field values" still gives the bare numbers.

entries.title: The signs say what they say
entries.detail: Every scrolling marquee in both games now reads out its actual text. Open the screen a board stands on and you get the words: Rupture Farms telling you the profits justify the means, SoulStorm Brew insisting its spew is your brew, the tutorial boards explaining the controls. Switch on the "Displays" filter and a hover says it too. Oddysee's hint-fly swarms are in too, the ones that spell a phrase in mid-air while Abe chants at them. An Exoddus board that answers a switch shows both of its messages and says which state each belongs to, and a board that draws from a random pool lists what is in the pool. Search reads all of it, so half a remembered slogan finds the sign it was on. Some boards turn out to say nothing at all, and the map says so rather than staying quiet: 20 of Oddysee's 45 stand dark. Every one is in Rupture Farms Return, standing where a board taught you to hoist or sneak the first time through, blanked for your return.

entries.title: The whole game, drawn as one diagram
entries.detail: The map has always been able to say where one door leads. What it could never show you is the shape of the whole thing. A World graph button under the path list, or the v key, puts the map away and draws the game as a diagram. A column per level in the order you play them, and a box per path in the order you meet them. Between them runs a line for every door, express well, bird portal, teleporter and transition. Oddysee comes out at 74 boxes and 77 lines, Exoddus at 92 and 97. The lines wear the connection arrows' own colours, with an arrowhead where a link runs only one way, forty-one of them in all. What the games are built out of stops being a thing you have to remember. The Scrabanian Temple's Trials hall fans out to eight rooms, FeeCo Depot is a lobby and five terminals, and the SoulStorm Brewery is three hubs with fourteen zulags hanging off them. Exoddus turns out to be two games that never touch, nothing in the mines and the vaults connecting to anything in the depot, the barracks or the brewery. Hover a box for the place's full name, its note and every path it leads to, hover a line for what it is made of, and click a box to travel there. Fit scales the whole game into the window, and the address bar carries the diagram, so you can send somebody the shape of a game.

entries.title: The map draws without waiting for both games
entries.detail: Opening the map meant waiting for both games' data to arrive, all of it, before a single line was drawn. You were only ever looking at one of them. Exoddus alone is twice the size of Oddysee. The map now works out which game you are opening from the link and waits on that one, drawing as soon as it lands; the other downloads quietly behind it and its button appears when it arrives. On a slow mobile connection the blank canvas at the start is a little over half as long as it was. A search typed before the second game has landed says so on its summary line, and picks up the rest of the hits the moment they arrive.

entries.title: Save a whole path as one image
entries.detail: Saving the map as a picture has always meant saving the window: cropped to what was on screen, at whatever zoom was set. Fitting a whole level in meant zooming out until the artwork was mush. A second button beside it now draws the entire path into one image. Every screen goes in edge to edge at the artwork's own resolution, whatever the view happens to be showing. The overlays, markers and plotted route you have on are drawn over the top. Rupture Farms' widest path comes out 4416 by 720 pixels with all twenty of its screens on it. The largest path either game has, deep in the Necrum Mines, comes out 4416 by 3360 with thirty-seven. Hover marks stay out of it. A highlight ring, or the wires dimmed around the one you were pointing at, is the pointer talking, and it has no business in a picture you are about to share. And where a path really is too large for one image, which takes turning on the gaps between screens, the export scales it down to fit and says what it scaled to.

entries.title: The encyclopedia corrects twelve of its cards
entries.detail: Twelve object cards have been checked against the games' own code and corrected. Two change what you would do. A Slig's card said it shoots what it sees on its own plane, which reads as an invitation to step onto the other one. In fact a background Slig carries a second shot along the depth axis and snipes into the foreground, which is what the no-fire cover boxes are scattered about for. And the sacks and the grenade machine are not gated on what is in your hands but on every rock, bone, meat and grenade in existence, so a bone you dropped two screens back keeps the next bag shut. The rest were true but said too broadly: a shadow zone tints the plane it names rather than every sprite, a checkpoint can decline to save you, and several claimed a depth-plane rule the engine applies to almost everything.

entries.title: A key lists what is on the screen you are looking at
entries.detail: Asking what a screen holds has always meant clicking it, which left the keyboard no way to ask at all. Press L and the list opens for the screen nearest the middle of the view, with the keyboard already inside it. The camera's name and its object count come first, then Tab walks the rows, Enter jumps to the object one names, and Escape closes the list and hands the keyboard back to where it came from. Nearest rather than dead centre on purpose: a path's grid of screens is mostly empty space, so insisting on the exact middle would have refused on half of them.

entries.title: The map says where it is, out loud
entries.detail: To a screen reader this map was an unnamed picture that never seemed to change: nothing said which game, which level or which path was on it. It now says so on arrival: the game, the level's full name, the path and the name it carries, how many objects are on it, and whether it carries one of the notes the map keeps about odd places. The map itself is named with that same line instead of being anonymous. It is said once wherever you arrived from, a path button, a door, a shared link or the shuffle button, and holding the path keys down no longer talks over itself. Pressing i now puts the keyboard inside the place panel, so the level's full name, its section, its nickname and its note can be read there.

entries.title: Path buttons can follow the order you play
entries.detail: A level's path buttons have always followed the order the games store their paths in, which has little to do with walking the level. The Stock Yards list their entrance last, and Rupture Farms Return reads Zulag 2, 2, 2, 4, 3, 3 down its eighteen buttons before it ever reaches Zulag 1. Turn on "Paths in play order" in Settings and the paths are listed in the order you reach them instead. The way in comes first, then a walk of the doors, wells, portals and transitions out from it, with each area finished before the next begins. Necrum Mines opens on Tunnel 1 with its secret area beside it, and the Paramonian Temple lists the hub before its six trials. The Brewery reads its terminal, then each of its three hubs ahead of the zulags it opens.

entries.title: The offscreen note stops reading like a description
entries.detail: Hover an object anchored between camera windows and the tooltip says so: the map is drawing it over a neighbouring screen. That line was set exactly like the object's own description below it, so the two ran together as one paragraph with nothing to say which was which. The note is now a size smaller and a good deal fainter, keeping what the map has to say about its own drawing apart from what it has to say about the object.

entries.title: The object filters say what falls inside them
entries.detail: The Display toggles have explained themselves on hover for a while; the object filters beneath them did not, and they are the ones whose contents you cannot guess. Hover one now for what it holds: that the doors filter carries wells, portals and teleporters too, that the hazards include the orbs and claws that punish rather than kill, and what on earth is in "Meta / bounds / fx". On a phone the note appears as you tap.

entries.title: The gaps toggle is remembered like the rest
entries.detail: With "Remember display & object filters" on, the Display toggles come back the way you left them across visits. "Gaps between screens" did not: the choice was saved and then ignored on the way back in, so the map always reopened with the screens packed edge to edge. It now returns spread if that is how you left it.

entries.title: By the numbers says when its table is full
entries.detail: The counting table holds six object types, but the list below it gave no sign of that: a seventh tick undid itself the moment you made it, with nothing to say why. With six picked the rest of the list now greys out, so you see the limit instead of running into it. Drop one and the list comes back.

entries.title: This map is part of RetroAtlas
entries.detail: Oddworld Map now says where it belongs: it is part of RetroAtlas, a collection of interactive maps of classic games. The line sits in "About this map", at the foot of the sidebar, with a link to the rest of them. Nothing about this map changes; it keeps its own address and its own source.

entries.title: A copied object link says what it points at
entries.detail: Right-clicking an object to copy a link to it confirmed with "object link copied", which said nothing about which of the objects under the pointer it took. It names the one it linked now: "Mudokon link copied".

entries.title: The minimap comes to phones
entries.detail: The overview of the path in the lower-right corner, with your viewport drawn on it, was kept to wide screens, leaving it off the screens where a path is least likely to fit at once. It is there on phones now, and dragging it moves the view: one swipe across a path that panning crosses in a dozen. On a phone it steps aside while the screen list or By the numbers is up, and at any width it stays away while the whole path already fits.

entries.title: Going back closes the panel you are in
entries.detail: On a phone, going back is how you leave anything, but with What's New, Settings, About, the shortcut list or an object's encyclopedia card open, the browser had nowhere to go but off the map. And on a first visit, there was nowhere to come back from. Back now closes whichever panel is open, exactly as Escape and the × do, and leaves the map only once none is.

entries.title: Three fields stop showing where they mean nothing
entries.detail: A field the game only reads on some placements used to show on all of them. Exoddus's invisible wipe lines now show the block of switch ids they clear only on the six of twelve that clear anything, and the other six show the flag alone. The unmarked trip zones show their alarm flag on the 17 that raise it, 11 in Oddysee and 6 in Exoddus, and stay quiet on the 180 that leave it alone. A bird portal shows its Shrykull count only on the ten that grant the power, four in Oddysee and six in Exoddus.

entries.title: Collision lines answer the pointer where they bend
entries.detail: Hovering a floor, wall or ceiling tested the straight run between the line's two ends, but the map bends a line at every camera edge it crosses. The reading could come out of empty space while the line itself gave nothing back, and the ruler snapped to points the line never reaches. Both follow the line as drawn now. It shows on 42 lines in Oddysee and 749 in Exoddus.

entries.title: Objects half off their screen dotted the wrong half
entries.detail: An object straddling the top or left edge of its screen had its outline drawn the wrong way round: the part on screen came back dotted, the part out in the gap solid. Some pull ring ropes in Mudomo Vault showed it plainly. The box now takes its position from the screen it covers, so the dotting falls the right way and the wires, arrows and pointer all find it where it is drawn.

entries.title: Hover defaults, curated per object
entries.detail: What an object shows before you reach for the Fields picker is now curated type by type. Each type shows the mode that picks its machine, and the codes and counts that make a placement itself: a security door's password, a boom machine's grenades, a status board's headcount. It shows the direction fields that decide play too, like an enemy stopper's blocked side or a bird portal exit's facing. The switch ids the wiring overlay draws leave the list, since its arrows already say who sets what. Dead words, constant tuning timers and cosmetic offsets stay behind the picker, and an unused id left at zero no longer shows at all.

entries.title: The smallest updates say so
entries.detail: Thirty-nine entries here record a one-line fix, a flipped default or a small refinement, and on this page they looked exactly like the features they were listed beside. Each now carries a quiet Tiny next to its kind, the way the biggest carry Flagship at the other end of the scale, so the shape of a week's work reads at a glance. Nothing has left the feed: the smallest change keeps its date, its place and its paragraph, because a map that is tended every week should look like one.

entries.title: The wires are drawn before you ask for them
entries.detail: Switch wiring (the green lines from every lever, button and wheel to the doors, drills and walls answering its switch id) waited behind a Display toggle, so the map opened showing where things are and not what they do. It is on from the first visit now, and the toggle (or the w key) still switches it off. If you've chosen to remember your display settings, your own choice still wins.

entries.title: Take the whole map with you, before you lose signal
entries.detail: "Keep the map on this device" used to keep only what you had already looked at, which is no help when the place you need is one you have never opened. Switching it on now offers each game's artwork as a single download: about 65 MB for Oddysee, 137 MB for Exoddus, or both in one go. It runs in the background while you carry on browsing, and resumes where it left off if you stop it or lose the connection. Once it finishes, every screen of that game opens with no connection at all: on a plane, underground, or wherever the signal is not.

entries.title: See the gaps the games leave between screens
entries.detail: The map packs away the slack the games leave around each camera, so screens sit edge to edge. The new "Gaps between screens" toggle in Display spreads them onto the real grid instead. An Oddysee screen turns out to sit well inside its cell: 256 units of space to its left, 400 to its right, 120 above and 120 below. Exoddus leaves only 7 to the right and 20 below. Objects and collision lines left in a gap stop hovering over the neighbouring screen and sit where they really are. They stay dotted, because the games draw none of it and Abe is teleported straight across whenever the camera changes. Your view, ruler and route all survive the switch.

entries.title: Collision lines stop pretending the gap is floor
entries.detail: Objects already showed where they run off their own screen. Now collision lines do too: a floor, wall or ceiling goes dotted where it crosses the gap between cameras, and stays solid where you can really stand on it. One that crosses the gap and carries on into the next screen stays solid throughout, since the packed map gives that gap no width. It shows most in Oddysee, whose wide gap dots 1740 of its 2895 lines, against 812 of Exoddus' 6645.

entries.title: Objects spilling off their screen show where they end
entries.detail: Both games address their cameras on a grid coarser than the screen you see, and the designers sometimes ran an object into the leftover gap. The map lays screens out edge to edge, so that part of it gets drawn over the neighbouring screen and has always looked misplaced. An outline now goes hollow and dotted exactly where the object leaves its own screen, and stays solid where it covers screen you can see. Oddysee's gap is 656 units wide and swallows 276 objects whole: those are dotted throughout, and their row in a screen's object list is tagged. Abe never walks that gap either, since the game teleports him straight across it whenever the camera changes.

entries.title: A shared link uses the game's own coordinates
entries.detail: Copy a link and the view it carries, along with any route you have plotted, is written in the coordinates Oddworld itself uses: the same numbers the readout in the map's corner shows. A link now points at a place in the game rather than at a place on the map, so how the map lays its screens out can change without moving it.

entries.title: Exoddus screens are no longer squashed
entries.detail: Exoddus addresses its cameras on a grid a little larger than the screen you actually see, and the map had been treating that whole grid cell as visible artwork. Everything on an Exoddus screen was therefore pulled toward its top-left corner: up to 7 pixels across and 20 down, worst at the bottom of a screen. Floors sat below their collision lines, status boards floated off their panels, and objects near a screen's edge drifted off it. Screens now sit 1:1 on their artwork, as Oddysee's already did.

entries.title: The Mines' two tunnels are joined at last
entries.detail: Necrum Mines Tunnel 2 had no door joining it to Tunnel 1, because the game carries you across in a cutscene instead. The level loader that runs that cutscene now names its destination and follows like any door.

entries.title: Water is a provocation, not decoration
entries.detail: The encyclopedia called Exoddus' falling water purely cosmetic, which it is not. The game counts a soaking as a slap, so the Mudokon under it turns angry and throws a punch.

entries.title: Objects filed under the wrong filter move
entries.detail: The security orb that zaps Abe for chanting sat among the switches and levers. The security claw and the sweeping motion detectors sat in the meta bucket, hidden by default. The orb and the claw both punish Abe, and the detectors raise the alarm that fetches something which will, so all three are hazards now. The boxes that wipe a range of switch ids join the switches, where the rest of the wiring logic already lives. The FeeCo train door leaves Doors / Transitions for meta: it is a graphic, and the ordinary door beside it is what carries the ride.

entries.title: Sacks and vending machines get a filter of their own
entries.detail: The sacks and machines that stock Abe up now have a filter of their own, "Pickups / dispensers", on by default: rock, meat and bone sacks, grenade machines and brew dispensers. What is left of that bucket becomes "Displays": scrolling boards, status lamps and meters, and hint flies.

entries.title: The biggest additions now wear a flagship badge
entries.detail: Seventeen entries so far in this feed are not ordinary updates. They are the features the map was built around, and they now say so: a shifting foil badge beside the NEW label and a lit rail down the entry. The row above gains a flagship chip to match; switch the other three off and what remains is the shortest possible history of the site.

entries.title: Object tooltips separate description from data
entries.detail: An object's hover tooltip now reads in layers. The type description leans into an italic aside, and field values brighten against their dimmed names, so the words and numbers that vary from one placement to the next are what catch the eye. Lines also wrap between whole fields now, never splitting a value from its name.

entries.title: Drill directions read as words
entries.detail: An Exoddus drill's start direction now shows as down, right or left. The drill's own direction enum sits outside the headers the builder reads types from, so the field shipped as a bare number that the usual left-and-right convention misread: its common value means down, not left.

entries.title: Every object field explains itself
entries.detail: The field glossary is complete: every stored field of every object in both games now carries a plain-English definition. Hover the dotted underline in the screen list or the Fields picker (or tap it on a phone) for what the field means, in frames and grid squares where the engine counts that way, with its possible values listed. Fields the games' code never reads say so outright, so a custom-level builder knows which knobs are real. Five hundred and sixty-five definitions, up from forty-four.

entries.title: Every object type explains itself
entries.detail: The map now carries an encyclopedia: one curated paragraph per object type, researched from the games' reverse-engineered code, telling you what a ZBall, a SlapLock or a Greeter actually is and does. Hovering an object opens with that story's first sentence. The ⓘ beside any object in the screen list, or next to a type in the Fields panel, opens the full card. That gives the whole entry, how many are placed in each game (counted live, demo paths noted apart), what the type's stored fields mean, and a link that finds every one of them with search. All 139 object types across both games are covered.

entries.title: The map works offline now
entries.detail: Switch on "Keep the map on this device" in Settings and the app itself (page, code and data) is stored alongside the artwork of the screens you visit. With no connection at all, the map opens and works, every place you've browsed included. Online, nothing changes: you always get the freshest version, and the stored copy refreshes as you browse. The setting used to keep only the artwork; it now keeps the whole map, and turning it off still removes everything.

entries.title: The Display toggles wear their keys
entries.detail: Each Display toggle with a keyboard shortcut now shows it as a small key at the row's edge, and the key lights up while it's held. The shortcuts are learnable right where the toggles live, not just in the ? list.

entries.title: The Display toggles explain themselves
entries.detail: Hover any toggle under Display for a short note on what it draws and how to read it: which colour marks a ceiling, what the wiring spotlight does, where the ruler snaps, how far a Slig will patrol. On a phone the note appears as you tap the toggle, so it explains itself in the same gesture that flips it. No more switching all ten on to find out which is which.

entries.title: What does that lever do? Switch wiring, drawn
entries.detail: Every lever, button, wheel and pressure plate in these games flips a numbered switch, and a door, drill, electric wall, trapdoor or spawner can be wired to listen for one. The new Switch wiring toggle under Display (or the w key) draws those connections as green dotted lines, including the logic gates Exoddus hides between them, where several work wheels have to agree before a door will open. Hover a wired object to spotlight just its own wires, with arrowheads showing which way the signal runs. The tooltip spells out what it sets and what it answers to, including wires that reach another path of the level. Wires run between markers you can see, so a hidden category takes its wires with it. The timer relays and pull rings now file under Switches / levers, green and on by default, so the objects doing the wiring are visible out of the box.

entries.title: A minimap for the paths that outgrow the window
entries.detail: Zoomed in on a big path, there was nothing that said where in it you are or how much lies off-screen. Now a small overview sits in the lower-right corner: the path's camera grid, with a rectangle showing exactly what the window sees. Click or drag inside it to jump the view around. It appears only when some of the path is off-screen, steps aside while the By-the-numbers panel is open.

entries.title: Routes go through doors now
entries.detail: The route planner used to stop at the edge of the path you plotted it on; a run through a door was two routes and a sum done by hand. Now, with the planner armed, clicking a door, well, portal or teleporter closes the leg on it, rides it, and keeps plotting where you land. The line breaks at each crossing (the travel between the halves isn't walked) and the bar totals the whole journey and says how many paths it spans. Undo takes a crossing back whole, and the back button retraces every ride with the route as it stood. A shared link carries the whole journey: whoever opens one can walk it, moving among its paths by button, by door or by the back button without losing it. Only wandering somewhere the route never goes clears it, and the back button brings it back.

entries.title: The pens enemies patrol are on the map
entries.detail: Sligs and Scrabs are penned in by invisible bound markers, and until now those hid in the default-off Meta bucket looking like every other grey box. A new Display toggle, Enemy patrol pens (or the p key), draws them as dashed posts on the exact boundary the game enforces, each with a small foot pointing into the pen. Hovering a Slig or a Slig spawner shades the span it patrols, edge to edge between its own pair of posts, matched the way the game itself does it: by the slig id both ends carry. Scrab bounds carry no such id, so Scrabs get their posts and no shading. The posts need Enemies / spawners on, and the toggle is off by default, since hundreds of posts are a lot of ink for anyone not reading patrol ranges.

entries.title: Count anything, everywhere, at a glance
entries.detail: A new "By the numbers" button under the Objects filters opens a panel that counts. Pick up to six object types and read how many stand on the screen under your view, on the current path, in the level, and across the whole game. The figures re-derive themselves as you switch paths, follow doors or shuffle. Counts read the data rather than the display, so a type whose filter is off still counts, and the demo-paths setting is honoured with a note on what the hidden copies hold. Click a type's name in the table to drop it.

entries.title: A shuffle button drops you somewhere odd
entries.detail: Beside the place chip in the map's corner sits a new shuffle button: one press and the map takes you to a random screen; either game, any level, weighted by nothing but how many screens a place has. The chip tells you where you landed, and the browser's back button brings you home. Exoddus' demo copies stay out of the draw unless the demo-paths setting lists them.

entries.title: Measurements snap to what you aim at
entries.detail: The ruler's ends and the route planner's waypoints now stick to the nearest object center (and to collision-line ends while those are shown) within a few screen pixels. Door-to-door distances and mine-to-ledge legs come out exact instead of eyeballed, and since the radius follows the screen rather than the world, zooming in shrinks it away whenever free placement is what you want.

entries.title: Search can name a single screen
entries.detail: The Places group answered to a level or a path; now it goes one screen deeper. Type a camera code (r1 p15 c3, or a full camera name like r1p15c03 straight off the grid overlay) and the screen itself comes back as a place; clicking it centers that very camera. Screens only answer when the query names one, so searching brewery still brings back the Brewery and its paths rather than a hundred screens.

entries.title: The corner readout counts grid squares
entries.detail: The readout in the map's bottom-right corner has always tracked the pointer's world position. It now also says where the pointer stands within its screen, in the games' own 25-unit grid squares (the unit the ruler already speaks). Read it off the corner instead of arming the ruler to count squares.

entries.title: Oddysee's main menu joins the map
entries.detail: Every level of both games is now on the map. Oddysee's menu level was the one hole: the game builds it from eighteen screens of its own, but the layout notes the map reads its grids from say nothing about it, so it was skipped. Its grid is now read off the level itself, and the two transitions out of Rupture Farms and Monsaic Lines that lead there (the ones the attract-mode demos take when they finish) follow like any other link instead of reporting a place the map could not show you.

entries.title: Search finds places, not just what is in them
entries.detail: Search could find every Slig in either game but not one of the rooms they stand in, so the level and path buttons were the only way to navigate to a specific place. Typing monsaic or feeco returned nothing; zulag 2 was worse, coming back with status boards from seven levels because some boards store a zulag number. Places now come back as their own group above the objects. A level or a path answers to its name and nickname, so "Tear X-Tractor" finds the Brewery's zulag 4. It answers to its code too, so BR P19 goes straight there. A level's name finds what is inside it too: "paramonia temple" brings back the Paramonian Temple first, then its entrance, the path outside its door and its boulder trials. Clicking any of them takes you there, a level opening on the first path it lists.

entries.title: The buttons say where you are going by default
entries.detail: "Show full names" started off, so the level and path buttons opened as bare short codes and a name only arrived if you went looking for the setting. Enough of the map is named now (the temple trials, the zulags, the nicknames players gave the Brewery) that the codes were hiding the better label. Full names are now on from the first visit, and the setting is still there to go back to the codes.

entries.title: Nine Brewery zulags carry the nickname players gave them
entries.detail: SoulStorm Brewery numbers its zulags and never names them, so a player who has just dodged their way through a room full of drills knows exactly where they are but might not remember which zulag it is. Its players filled the gap: the Oddworld Wiki names each zulag as a sector, and nine of those describe what is really in the area. Zulag 3, Industrial Machines, runs more drills than anywhere else in the level. Zulag 6, Electrical Devices, is strung with eleven electric walls. Zulag 7, Blind Mudokon, is worked by the only three blind Mudokons in the brewery. Zulag 12, Tear Extractors, has TEAR X-TRACTOR painted on the wall under the rig. Those nicknames now sit beside the number, in the panel behind the map's chip and in a path button's tooltip, and on the button itself with "Show full names" on. They read dimmed, because a nickname is the players' name for the place and not the game's. The other five carry none, at least for now: a nickname only arrives where an area has something you would recognise it by.

entries.title: A link to an object says which object
entries.detail: Opening a link to a specific object rings it with a marker, which is easy to follow on a quiet screen and much less so on one carrying two dozen things. The name was only ever in the URL, where it can be missed easily. The map now names what the marker is on, in a message at the bottom, the way it already told you when the object turned out not to be there.

entries.title: Read only the kind of update you came for
entries.detail: The tags under this panel's masthead now switch each kind of update in or out of the list below: turn "fixed" off to read only what has been added and improved, or leave them all on for the whole story. The choice is forgotten as soon as the panel closes, so a filter set months ago can never quietly hide the news.

entries.title: The newest toast really lands at the bottom
entries.detail: When several toasts stack, the newest was quietly appearing above the older ones instead of taking the bottom slot where a lone toast stands, so the reaction to what you just did moved around depending on how many messages were up. The newest now always lands at the bottom and pushes the older ones up, the way the stack was described when it shipped.

entries.title: "Reduce motion" now stops all of the motion
entries.detail: If your system asks for reduced motion, the map turned off its animations, except two that slipped through. A dialog still faded in over about a fifth of a second, though it closed instantly, and on a phone the menu drawer still slid in from the side. Both now simply appear and disappear, which is what the setting asks for.

entries.title: Object tooltips are no longer buried
entries.detail: An object's tooltip is a wide box set just below and right of the pointer, so pointing anywhere near the edge of the map left it sitting beneath whatever else was on screen. The description of the very thing you were pointing at came out underneath the screen list, the panel behind the corner chip, the route planner's bar or a passing message. Tooltips now draw above all four.

entries.title: The buttons and the search box use the map's own font
entries.detail: A browser hands buttons and text boxes a font of their own unless the page says otherwise, and this page only said so in some places. So the game, level and path buttons, the search box and its scope filters, the rows in a screen's object list and the close button on every panel were drawing in the browser's font rather than the map's. So were the export button and the route planner's undo and clear. They all match now.

entries.title: The map says what it is, and where it comes from
entries.detail: A fan project ought to say so out loud rather than leave you to guess. "About this map", at the foot of the sidebar, now opens a short panel. It says that this is an unofficial, fan-made map, that Oddworld and its characters and designs are Oddworld Inhabitants' trademarks, and that the project is not affiliated with, endorsed or sponsored by them. It also credits the AliveTeam / alive_reversing project, whose reverse-engineering of the disc formats is what makes any of this readable, and links the map's own source code for anyone who wants to see how it is put together.

entries.title: Field definitions open on a tap, not just a hover
entries.detail: A field name with a dotted underline (in the screen list, and in the Fields panel in the sidebar) explains itself: what the field means, and what each of its values stands for. That explanation used to be the browser's own hover tooltip, which a phone or a tablet never shows at all, so on touch the underline promised something it could not deliver. Tapping one now opens the definition, and the tap still does whatever it was going to do: tick the field in the panel, or jump to the object in the screen list. On a mouse it appears the moment you point at it rather than after the browser's pause, and the list of values reads as its own line under the definition.

entries.title: The endgame areas get their own names
entries.detail: Thirteen Exoddus areas the endgame sends you back to were named after the half of the level they sit in rather than after themselves, so a room read "Mudanchee Vault Ender: Scrab Nest" and led with a word out of the developers' notes. They now go by their own names (Scrab Nest, Dripik's War Room, the Executive Office) while which half of the level you are in is still there to read: it sits above the path name in the panel behind the corner chip, and in the tooltip of the path button. Nothing was dropped, only untangled.

entries.title: The settings you have changed say so
entries.detail: A setting that is off because it ships that way looked exactly like one you switched off yourself, so there was no telling which of the eight settings you had ever touched. A setting you have changed now says on the right of its row what it was to begin with: "off by default" where you turned it on, "on by default" where you turned it off. One you have left alone says nothing, so what is written down the right-hand side is the list of what you changed.

entries.title: Settings come in three groups
entries.detail: The eight settings sat in one column with a paragraph under each, which had grown long enough that the panel scrolled before you reached the end of it. They are now sorted into what is saved on this device, what the buttons say, and what the map tells you about objects, under headings that read like the sidebar's own. The panel is a little wider to match, so on a desktop the whole list fits without scrolling. Nothing changed about what any setting does.

entries.title: The areas you can never walk to are hidden
entries.detail: A fifth of Exoddus' path buttons led to places the game never lets you visit: 25 copies of real areas, kept on the disc for the demos that play on the title screen while nobody presses a button. They cluttered every level's buttons and every search, so the map now leaves them out. "Show demo paths" in Settings brings them back for the curious, and a link to one opens it either way, so a shared screen never leads nowhere and the chip in the corner of the map says what you are looking at. The map spots them the way the game does, by the spawn point each demo starts from, so nothing was marked by hand.

entries.title: Links that go nowhere stop claiming Necrum Mines
entries.detail: Sixty-one links in Exoddus (doors, teleporters, express wells and bird portals) claimed to lead to Necrum Mines from another level, and not one of them meant it. A link the designers never pointed anywhere keeps the address it was born with, and that address reads as the Mines: a door in the Mudanchee Vaults offered to take you there and did, and twenty-six express wells all offered the ride to the same opening screen. The map now believes a destination in another level only where the door, teleporter, well or portal it pairs with is really there, and an express well takes whichever side of its switch leads somewhere, so the eight wells of the Slig Barracks hub connect to their partners across the room, and the vault trial wells to theirs. A link with nowhere real to go offers no follow, names no destination and draws no arrow, while the fields the game stores for it stay on show. Four paths in the Mines also lose the "entry point" badge they wore on the strength of a dead link alone.

entries.title: Full names on the buttons read as names
entries.detail: With "Show full names" on, every button wrapped its name in brackets, which reads as an aside rather than as the label it is, and a path whose name carries brackets of its own ([Demo] Annex 8: Slogs Attack) came out with two sets nested. The name now follows the short code after a dash instead.

entries.title: The map says where you are, and what is odd about it
entries.detail: A chip in the map's top-left corner now names the level and path you are looking at, wherever you arrived from. Click it, or press i, and it tells you the level's full name, whether the game ever arrives at this path from another level, and, on the paths that have something odd about them, a short remark on what that is. Thirteen Exoddus paths carry one so far, each marked by a dot on the chip. There is the Brewery's zulag 13, which almost every board in it misprints as 14 (a developer slip corrected for the Japanese release), and the arch out of zulag 11 that repeats the mistake. There are nine screens furnished with another level's artwork, eight of them secret areas, from the Slig Barracks hidden in the Necrum jungle to the railway depot tucked inside a Paramite trial. And there is the Mines' escape route, the boiler room you already crossed screen for screen, and FeeCo's terminal 3, the one terminal the game never numbers.

entries.title: Links that leave the map say what is out there
entries.detail: Two objects in Oddysee, one in Rupture Farms and one in Monsaic Lines, point at a level the map doesn't draw. Hovering either already told you its name and that it isn't on the map; it now also says what it is: the main menu, where the game's title-screen demos return when they finish, which is why those two links exist at all.

entries.title: Every Exoddus area now has a name
entries.detail: The rest of Exoddus follows the Brewery: all eighty-six paths across the Mines, Necrum, both vaults, FeeCo Depot, the Slig Barracks, Bonewerkz and the final boiler room now say where you are. Where the game paints the answer on the wall, that is what you get: the mine's numbered tunnels, the barracks' blocks, FeeCo's numbered terminals, each read off the boards and arches in the artwork. Where it paints nothing, as in the two vaults, the name comes from matching each path's contents against a walkthrough, so the vault trials are numbered the way players number them. Eighteen more paths turn out to be demo copies you can never walk to, marked [Demo], sixteen of them under the names the game gives those demos.

entries.title: The Brewery's zulags have names
entries.detail: Exoddus names none of the twenty-eight paths in SoulStorm Brewery, so the map could only number them. Each now says which zulag it is, read off the "employees this zulag" boards on the walls and checked against the doors each hub opens. Seven of the paths turn out to be copies of a zulag that the game only ever plays back as a demo, unreachable however you play; those are marked [Demo], four of them under the names the game gives those demos. One board is not to be trusted: most of Zulag 13's read 14, a known developer slip, so the map calls it 13.

entries.title: Portals that go nowhere stop naming a destination
entries.detail: In Exoddus, the bird portals that don't travel anywhere (the ones Mudokons fly up through, and the ones that grant Shrykull) nearly all claimed to lead to Necrum Mines P1 C1, and offered a link there. The levels do store a destination for them, but the game never reads it: such a portal closes where it stands and never moves Abe, so the stored value is scratch, usually the untouched default that points at the first screen of the first level. All 118 of them now show no destination at all. Genuine travel portals are unchanged.

entries.title: Tab skips the closed sidebar
entries.detail: With the sidebar collapsed, the Tab key still travelled through every one of its buttons (some fifty of them) before reaching the map. It now goes straight past, and closing the sidebar leaves Tab where it left off, on the menu button.

entries.title: A failed PNG export says so
entries.detail: "Export view as PNG" can fail when the browser won't encode a picture. It used to do nothing at all, no file and no reason given. It now says the export failed.

entries.title: The page can be zoomed on phones
entries.detail: The site used to refuse the browser's own zoom, so the sidebar, the settings dialog, What's New and the screen list were stuck at whatever size your phone picked. Pinch any of them now and the page zooms like on any other site. Two fingers on the map still zoom the map, with one exception: while the page itself is zoomed they zoom the page back out, so a zoom you took to read a panel is never left stranded once the panel closes.

entries.title: Toasts stack instead of talking over each other
entries.detail: The little messages (toasts) at the bottom of the map had one place to stand, so when a link had two things to say (for example that the object it named isn't there, and that the route it carried arrived short) the second wiped the first out on the spot. They now stack, up to three at a time with the rest counted on a badge above, each with a bar draining to show how long it has left. They also linger a little longer than they used to.

entries.title: The view holds still when the window changes size
entries.detail: Resizing the window, rotating a phone, or opening and closing the sidebar used to slide the map sideways, because the view was pinned by its top-left corner: whatever you were looking at drifted off, and on a narrow window the sidebar alone could push it out of sight. The middle of the view now stays where it is.

entries.title: Object links keep their marker
entries.detail: A link to a specific object matched its name exactly, so one that had passed through anything that lowercases URLs opened the right view and then quietly dropped the marker. Names now match whatever their capitals, as the game and level codes always have. And when the object really isn't there (a hand-typed link, or one aimed at something a data rebuild has moved) the map still goes to the spot the link named, rings it, and says which object it expected.

entries.title: Links still work when sharing rewrites them
entries.detail: Some apps rewrite the part of a URL after the # when you share it, leaving %2F where every slash used to be. A link that came through one of those opened the default view instead of the place it named. The rewriting is now undone before the link is read.

entries.title: Route links survive being shortened
entries.detail: Chat apps and forums sometimes shorten a long URL, and a route that lost its tail could still be read as a complete one, drawn a leg or two short with no sign anything was missing. A shortened route link is now recognised: it opens with the waypoints that did arrive and says how many didn't ("route link cut short: 13 of 16 waypoints").

entries.title: Shared links open the same on any screen
entries.detail: A link carried the top-left corner of the window it was copied from, so opening it on a narrower screen (a phone, a smaller window, an embed in a forum post) slid the view sideways. At a common zoom the drift was more than a whole camera screen, enough to leave what was being pointed at off the edge entirely. Links now carry the middle of the view, and whatever window opens one works out its own corner.

entries.title: "Export view as PNG" saves the file in every browser
entries.detail: The export could end with nothing saved and no error, depending on the browser: the image was thrown away the moment the download was handed over, which Firefox and Safari take as a cancelled transfer. It is now kept until the browser has actually taken it, however long a save dialog sits open.

entries.title: Object tooltips stay on screen near the edges
entries.detail: Hovering an object low on the map cut the tooltip off at the bottom of the window, with no way to scroll it back into view. It now flips above the pointer when there is no room below. Near the right edge it stays beside what it describes instead of jumping left, and on a narrow phone screen it no longer starts off the left edge.

entries.title: The marker on a shared object link settles down
entries.detail: Opening a link to a specific object rings it with a pulsing marker that holds until you have seen it. On a page nobody touched it held forever, redrawing the map every frame (a quiet battery drain on a tab left open, phones especially). Moving the pointer now counts as seeing it, and the marker settles by itself after half a minute either way.

entries.title: Measurements no longer linger after you move on
entries.detail: A line drawn with the ruler stayed on screen when you switched path with [ and ], followed a door or changed game, sitting over the new screens measuring nothing, and after a game switch reading the wrong distance outright. It now clears whenever you move somewhere else.

entries.title: Most object fields now say what they mean
entries.detail: The hover definitions cover nearly everything an object shows by default: what a switch number wires together, where a hoist carries Abe, what a lever's action does to its switch, a Mudokon's work and mood, a Slig's start state and how long it waits before shooting, a Scrab's patrol style, and whether a door, trap door, electric wall or saw starts on. Hover any field name with a dotted underline to read its meaning and every value it can take. A handful whose meaning isn't settled yet still have none.

entries.title: Background objects are cued by the right plane
entries.detail: The dimmed dashed outline that marks the background plane read a raw value that doesn't mean the same thing for every object, so a few kinds were cued backwards: foreground invisible switches were dashed while background ones weren't, and half-scale door flames were missed. Each object's own scale meaning now decides it.

entries.title: Hover a field name to learn what it means
entries.detail: Field names in the screen list and the Fields panel can now carry a plain-English definition and their full list of possible values. Hover a name shown with a dotted underline to read it. This starts small (only a few fields are described so far) and will grow over time.

entries.title: Objects show more at a glance
entries.detail: Hovering an object now surfaces the fields that matter for how it behaves, without turning anything on. A door shows whether it starts open or locked, an electric wall or trap door whether it starts on, a bird portal who it's for, a Glukkon or Crawling Slig its type and state, a MeatSaw its speed. "Show more object fields" still reveals everything else and lets you pick per type.

entries.title: Background-plane objects stand out
entries.detail: Objects sitting on the half-scale background plane are now drawn dimmed with a dashed outline (the same "dashed means background" cue the collision lines already use) so you can tell a foreground hazard from one tucked in the back when reading a screen or planning a route.

entries.title: Search several terms at once
entries.detail: Search now takes more than one term. A space means all must match, so "Mudokon state=chisle" finds only the chiselling Mudokons (before, you had to type the terms exactly as stored and in order, otherwise the search found nothing). A comma or the word "or" means any: "Slig, Slog" finds both. Each matched term is highlighted in the result.

entries.title: Search follows the raw-values setting
entries.detail: With "Show raw field values" on, search now matches the raw numbers you actually see. For example, start_state=3 finds the chasing Sligs, where before you had to type the translated word even though the rows showed numbers. Matched rows no longer show the value twice, and the highlight lands on it. With the setting off, search works on the translated words as before.

entries.title: Field changes reach open search results and screen lists
entries.detail: When you tick a field in the Fields panel, or turn "Show more object fields" on or off, any search results and screen lists you already have open now update right away instead of waiting for a re-open.

entries.title: Configure an object's fields where you found it
entries.detail: With "Show more object fields" on, every object in a screen's list gets a ⚙ button. Tap it to jump straight to that type's row in the Fields panel, so you set up a Slig's fields right where you're looking at one instead of hunting for it in the sidebar.

entries.title: Press "m" to measure
entries.detail: The ruler now has a keyboard shortcut, "m" for "measure". Tap it and drag to measure a distance without reaching for the sidebar toggle.

entries.title: Connection arrows shown by default
entries.detail: The map now opens with connection arrows on, so a screen's doors, wells, portals and transitions show where they lead at a glance. Press "a" or untick "Connection arrows" to turn them off. If you've chosen to remember your display settings, your own choice still wins.

entries.title: Objects and their fields sorted by name
entries.detail: The Fields panel now lists object types alphabetically, and each type's fields are alphabetical too (in the picker, tooltips and the screen list) instead of the game's internal order, so whatever you're after is where you'd expect it.

entries.title: The last raw objects now decode too
entries.detail: The object types that still showed only raw numbers now decode fully (hoists, lifts and pulleys, security claws and motion detectors, sound and zone triggers, shadow and light effects, meat and bone sacks, and the rest) so "Show more object fields" and search reach every gameplay object on the map. Continue zones now name their checkpoint number.

entries.title: Object fields read in plain language
entries.detail: Object fields now read as words instead of raw numbers, taken straight from the labels the developers wrote in the game's own code: on/off fields as true/false, a door's state (open, closed, hub door closed), an enemy spawner's start state read like a Slig's (patrol, sleeping, listening to glukkon), which way a hoist is grabbed, and dozens more per game. See them via "Show more object fields" or search; "Show raw field values" turns it all back to the numbers.

entries.title: See the raw numbers behind the labels
entries.detail: A new "Show raw field values" setting (off by default) swaps the friendly translations for the exact values the game stores (1/0 instead of true/false, a Slig's start_state as a number, a Mudokon's job as 1 rather than "sit scrub"). Handy if you're building custom levels or just curious what's under the hood. Search still understands the translated text either way.

entries.title: Every object's fields, not just creatures'
entries.detail: "Show more object fields" now reaches well beyond Mudokons and enemies: doors, switches, levers, mines, wells and the rest of the game's gameplay objects reveal what the developers stored on them (a door's lock state and which hubs it links, a switch's wiring, a mine's setup, and much more). Pick the fields you care about per type in the Fields panel, or just search for them.

entries.title: Exoddus measurements read true world units
entries.detail: The ruler and the route planner measured on the artwork, and Exoddus artwork squeezes each screen's 375×260 world units into 368×240 pixels, so lengths read up to 8% short, and hovering a collision line (which has always measured the real coordinates) disagreed with the ruler over the same wall. Both tools now convert to world units: a full Exoddus screen measures 375 across (exactly 15 grid squares) and 260 down, and all the readouts agree. Oddysee numbers were already exact and are unchanged.

entries.title: Every object field, yours to pick
entries.detail: Hover a Slig and you'll now see how it attacks, for example shoot_on_sight_delay=0 means it shoots the instant it sees you, with no "FREEZE!" warning - a nasty surprise at some screens. And there's much more underneath: turn on "Show more object fields" in Settings and a "Fields" panel appears in the sidebar, listing the object types on the current screen. Expand a type (Slig, Mudokon, ...) and tick exactly the fields you want in its tooltips and the screen list, with the notable ones pre-checked and "all" / "reset" shortcuts per type; your picks are remembered per game. Search always reaches every field even when it's hidden, so shoot_on_sight_delay=0 finds every ambush Slig in a level - and a result matched on a hidden field shows that field on the row.

entries.title: See how enemies start out
entries.detail: Hover a Slig or Slog (or search for one) to read its starting state: whether a Slig starts off patrolling or sleeping, whether a Slog starts asleep, and the switch id that wakes a Slog into anger where one is wired. Try searching start_state=sleeping or asleep=true to spot the dormant ones.

entries.title: Mudokons show what they're doing
entries.detail: Hover a Mudokon (or search for one) to see its decoded state, straight from the disc: in Oddysee its job (standing scrub, sitting scrub, or the sitting chant that marks the Monsaic natives) and in Exoddus its work state (chiselling, scrubbing, angry worker, ring-giver) and mood (normal, angry, sad, wired, sick). Try searching emotion=sad or job=sit chant.

entries.title: Plot a route and share it as a link
entries.detail: The new "Route planner" display toggle (or the r key) turns clicks into waypoints: every leg is labelled with its length, and a bar at the top totals the route in world units and grid squares. This is the ruler's big sibling, made for planning and practising runs. Backspace (or the bar's undo) removes the last point. The whole route travels in the page address, so copying the link shares it exactly as plotted and it shows up in PNG exports too; whoever opens it can still click doors and browse freely, the route stays put until they switch paths or clear it.

entries.title: The ruler keeps its crosshair
entries.detail: Arming the ruler turns the cursor into a crosshair, but the first mouse move used to snap it straight back to the ordinary pointer. The crosshair now stays for as long as the ruler is armed.

entries.title: Oddysee's areas carry their community names
entries.detail: Most paths in Abe's Oddysee now have a name (the temple trials, the Free-Fire Zone crossings, the bell towers, the nests) drawn from New 'n' Tasty's chapter names and community walkthroughs. Hover a path button (or turn on "Show full names" in Settings) to see them; the few names the game defines itself, like the zulags, stay exactly as the disc says.

entries.title: Doors to nowhere explain themselves
entries.detail: Some doors point at places the map doesn't render: two Oddysee transitions lead to S1, the main-menu level where the title-screen demos return, and dozens of Exoddus one-way doors (the kind that shut behind Abe) carry placeholder destinations like MI P0. Hovering one now says where it leads and that it's off the map, instead of offering a follow that went nowhere (or worse, dropped you on the wrong path).

entries.title: See a path's whole circulation as arrows
entries.detail: The new "Connection arrows" display toggle (or the a key) draws every door, express well, bird portal, teleporter and path transition linked to where it leads, turning the path into a readable routing flowchart. Two-way pairs collapse into one double-headed arrow, transitions to other paths show as short labelled stubs, colours tell the kinds apart, and hovering an object spotlights just its own arrows.

entries.title: Hover a door to see its other end
entries.detail: Hovering a linked object (a door, teleporter, well or portal) puts a dashed outline on the object it leads to, whenever both ends sit on the current path. You see where you'd come out before committing to the click.

entries.title: Tap a screen to see everything on it
entries.detail: Click or tap a camera screen (anywhere that isn't a followable object) and a panel lists every object on that screen, grouped by category. Hovering a row outlines the object on the map, clicking it jumps straight there, and tapping an object opens the list scrolled to that object's row. On phones the panel is a bottom sheet that leaves the map visible - with no hover to inspect with, this is the way to see what a screen holds. A Settings switch turns it off.

entries.title: Embed the map in wikis and forums
entries.detail: Adding ?embed=1 to the address gives a view made to sit in an iframe: the map fills the frame, still fully interactive, with the sidebar starting tucked away behind its menu button. Pair it with any permalink and the embed opens exactly on the screen you mean; a corner button takes visitors to the full site at the very spot they're looking at.

entries.title: More keyboard shortcuts, and ? to see them all
entries.detail: Press [ and ] to step through the current level's paths, and g, c and f flip the camera grid, collision lines and foreground masks without a trip to the sidebar. Press ? for a card listing every shortcut. Arrows still pan, + and - zoom, / jumps to search.

entries.title: Copy a link to the view you're looking at
entries.detail: The chain button in the top-right corner puts a permalink to the exact spot on screen on your clipboard. The address bar has always carried this link, but on phones (especially with the map opened as an installed app) there may be no address bar to copy from.

entries.title: Screens you've visited can load instantly on your next visit
entries.detail: Turn on "Cache screen artwork on this device" in Settings and visited screens stay stored locally (up to about 150 MB), so returning to the map doesn't re-download them screen by screen. Previously the whole map re-fetched after every site update. Off by default; switching it off removes everything stored.

entries.title: Express wells land on the arrival well
entries.detail: Following an express well now drops the highlight ring on the exact well you pop out of (matched by the same well id the game reads on arrival) instead of the middle of the destination screen. Wells whose switch-off state just bounces you back out now follow their real ride, including local rides to another screen of the same path.

entries.title: One-click reset for Display and Objects
entries.detail: A small reset in the Display and Objects headers puts that section back to its defaults, handy now that view options carry over between visits.

entries.title: Full game, level and path names on the buttons
entries.detail: Turn on "Show full names" in Settings and the game, level and path buttons expand into a list carrying their full names next to the short codes: "AO (Abe's Oddysee)", "R1 (Rupture Farms)", and the named path areas like the Rupture Farms Return zulags and the Exoddus enders.

entries.title: Pick up where you left off
entries.detail: Turning on "Remember last location" in Settings and reopening the site brings you back to the exact game, level, path and view you last had on screen. Opening a shared permalink still goes to the linked spot.

entries.title: Settings panel: view options are remembered
entries.detail: The gear button at the top of the sidebar opens the new Settings panel.
